newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus has good tourism prospects in 97 - officials.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus has good tourism prospects in 97 - officials.

text.p: Tourism arrivals for Cyprus are encouraging this year and could exceed 1996 figures, officials on the holiday island said on Thursday.

Tourists averaged two million in 1996 from around 2.2 million in 1995, while market prospects for this year were initially dampened by tension on the divided island, sparked by Cyprus's decision to purchase anti-aircraft missiles and Turkish threats to block their deployment.
"Personally, I am optimistic that we can reach last years' levels, at least," Kyriakos Christophi, the commerce, industry and tourism minister told hoteliers meeting in the capital Nicosia.

High costs and a lack of competitiveness of the tourism product on offer has been blamed for the stagnation of the industry, now diversifying from the staple of sun and sea to marine, sport and environmental tourism -- ecotourism.

"The weaknesses in the tourism product are not just on infrastructure, but on the lack of cleanliness, noise pollution, the burden on the environment and the exploitation of tourists," Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides said in an address.
"Above all we should retain our warmth and friendliness to the foreign visitor," he added.

Tourism represents 21 percent of gross domestic product in the south of the island. The figures do not include the northern third, which was invaded by Turkey in 1974 in response to a brief coup sponsored by the military ruling in Athens.
The southern areas are a popular holiday destination for Britons, Scandinavians and Germans.
Russians are also carving a niche for themselves in the market. Tourism officials expect a 20 percent increase on the 120,000 tourists who visited last year.
"There has been a deregulation of charter flights from Russia and Cyprus is a brand new destination for them," a tourism official told Reuters.

Tour operators and hoteliers themselves concede the island is more expensive than rival destinations in the region, and have emphasised the need to become more competitive and offer more quality service.
Cyprus is gradually moving away from the mass tourism which created the economic boom of the early eighties into quality tourism to attract tourists in a higher income bracket.
In an attempt to curb the number of hotels sprouting up on the coastlines, commercial banks are not allowed to finance construction of new establishments except those for ecotourism, said Clerides.
The government, he said, is sponsoring plans for development of marinas and golf courses, and is encouraging conference and sports tourism.
